title: Review: Oxidation states and half-equations; Group 2
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for Edexcel A-level Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: RX01#t1 term and clue written for the game; PT04#t4 term and clue written for the game; RX01#t4 term and clue written for the game; PT04#t3 term and clue written for the game. Questions: PT04#N.9, RX01#N.6a, PT04#N.15, RX01#N.13, PT04#N.5, RX01#N.11a, PT04#N.7, RX01#N.14, PT04#N.14. The matching task revisits terms from the worlds it reviews, in a new mix. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Redox
items.clue: A reaction in which loss and gain of electrons happen together.

items.label: Second ionisation energy
items.clue: Quantity for the change M⁺(g) → M²⁺(g) + e⁻, which falls down Group 2.

items.label: Reduction
items.clue: Gain of electrons, as when each O atom goes from 0 to −2 during rusting.

items.label: Oxidation
items.clue: Loss of electrons, as in M → M²⁺ + 2e⁻, where the state rises from 0 to +2.

questions.stem: Dilute sodium hydroxide is added to separate solutions of magnesium chloride and barium chloride. Dilute sulfuric acid is then added to fresh samples of each. Which observations are expected?

options.text: MgCl₂: white precipitate with NaOH only. BaCl₂: white precipitate with H₂SO₄ only.
MgCl₂: white precipitate with H₂SO₄ only. BaCl₂: white precipitate with NaOH only.
Both solutions give a white precipitate with NaOH and with H₂SO₄.
MgCl₂: white precipitate with both reagents. BaCl₂: no precipitate with either.

questions.explanation: Mg(OH)₂ is sparingly soluble but MgSO₄ is soluble. Ba(OH)₂ is soluble but BaSO₄ is insoluble.

questions.stem: Chlorine reacts with aqueous iron(II) ions: 2Fe²⁺(aq) + Cl₂(aq) → 2Fe³⁺(aq) + 2Cl⁻(aq). Which species is the oxidising agent in this reaction?

options.text: Fe²⁺, since it loses electrons and so is itself oxidised
Cl₂, since it gains electrons and so is itself reduced
Cl⁻, since it is the species holding the gained electrons
None, since no species here gains or loses any oxygen atoms

questions.explanation: Chlorine's oxidation number falls from 0 to −1: each Cl₂ gains two electrons from Fe²⁺. The species that accepts electrons is the oxidising agent.

questions.stem: Strontium reacts more vigorously than calcium with dilute hydrochloric acid. The sum of the first and second ionisation energies is 1735 kJ mol⁻¹ for calcium and 1614 kJ mol⁻¹ for strontium. Which explains the difference?

options.text: Strontium has a larger nuclear charge, so it attracts H⁺ ions from the acid more strongly.
Strontium's outer electrons are further out and more shielded, so less energy is needed to form Sr²⁺.
Strontium chloride is far more soluble than calcium chloride, so the metal surface stays clean.
Strontium atoms have more electrons, so each atom can give more electrons to the H⁺ ions.
Cl₂ + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br₂
2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO
2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂
NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂O

questions.explanation: O in H₂O₂ is −1 (a peroxide). It goes to −2 in H₂O (reduced) and to 0 in O₂ (oxidised): one element in one species, both ways.

questions.stem: Which equation shows the reaction of strontium with cold water?

options.text: Sr(s) + H₂O(l) → SrO(s) + H₂(g)
Sr(s) + 2H₂O(l) → Sr(OH)₂(aq) + H₂(g)
2Sr(s) + 2H₂O(l) → 2SrOH(aq) + H₂(g)
SrO(s) + H₂O(l) → Sr(OH)₂(aq)

questions.explanation: Sr forms Sr²⁺, so the hydroxide is Sr(OH)₂. Two water molecules supply two OH⁻ and release H₂.

questions.stem: In acidic solution, MnO₄⁻(aq) is reduced to Mn²⁺(aq) and Fe²⁺(aq) is oxidised to Fe³⁺(aq). In the balanced overall redox equation, what amount of Fe²⁺ reacts with 1 mol of MnO₄⁻?

options.text: 1 mol
5 mol
2 mol
3 mol

questions.explanation: Mn goes from +7 to +2, so each MnO₄⁻ gains 5 electrons; each Fe²⁺ loses 1. The iron half-equation is multiplied by 5.

questions.stem: Equal amounts of magnesium oxide and barium oxide are each shaken with water containing universal indicator. Which results are expected?

options.text: Both stay at about pH 7, because Group 2 oxides do not react with water.
MgO gives about pH 13 and BaO about pH 10, because Mg(OH)₂ is the more soluble.
Both give about pH 14, because every Group 2 hydroxide is a fully soluble strong alkali.
MgO gives about pH 10 and BaO about pH 13, because Ba(OH)₂ is far more soluble.

questions.explanation: More soluble hydroxide → more OH⁻ in solution → higher pH. Alkalinity increases down Group 2.

questions.stem: In the thermite reaction, aluminium reacts with iron(III) oxide: Fe₂O₃(s) + 2Al(s) → Al₂O₃(s) + 2Fe(l). What happens to the iron?

options.text: It loses electrons: iron is always oxidised when it reacts, as it does in rusting.
It gains electrons: its oxidation number falls from +3 to 0, and aluminium supplies them.
It loses electrons to aluminium, since aluminium gains the oxygen during the reaction.
It gains electrons: its oxidation number falls from +6 to 0, as Fe₂O₃ has two Fe atoms.

questions.stem: Which Group 2 carbonate decomposes at the lowest temperature, and why?

options.text: BaCO₃, because the large Ba²⁺ ion holds the carbonate ion only weakly.
BaCO₃, because barium is the most reactive metal in Group 2.
MgCO₃, because the small Mg²⁺ ion polarises the carbonate ion most.
MgCO₃, because Mg²⁺ carries a larger charge than the other Group 2 ions.

questions.explanation: Mg²⁺ has the highest charge density in the group. It distorts the CO₃²⁻ electron cloud most, weakening a C–O bond, so CO₂ is released at the lowest temperature.
